articles.headline: No agenda, no rush, no leaving San Francisco: Benchmark’s partners on investing in a frenzied market
keyFacts: Venture firm Benchmark announced $2 billion across two funds this summer, marking only the second time in its history of raising a smaller vehicle.
During an interview at TechCrunch Disrupt, Benchmark partners stated that the firm maintains a consistent pace of only two or three new bets per partner annually.
Benchmark partners explained that their Monday partner meetings continue to have no formal agenda to allow space for being reactive and discussing ongoing market changes.
body: The players sometimes change. I sat down with four of Benchmark’s partners three years ago, and three of those individuals are no longer with the firm. The capital commitments have changed, too. This summer, Benchmark announced $2 billion across two funds, marking only the second time in its 31-year history that it has veered from raising a far smaller vehicle.

But at this week’s TechCrunch Disrupt, the venture firm’s five partners convincingly portrayed a close-knit team that’s not about to put the pedal to the metal, even as many of their rivals do exactly that. The world may be speeding up, but they’re investing at the pace Benchmark always has: just two or three new bets per year per partner. The world is drowning in information, yet their Monday partner meetings still have no agenda. And while economic indicators point to trouble ahead, they don’t seem too bothered, seeing many of the warning signs as products of X-fueled hysteria.

Here’s what Benchmark’s five general partners — gathered together on our stage — had to say at the show. Some of the comments below have been edited for length and clarity; you can watch the full interview at the end of the article.
Benchmark has evolved in some ways, including a bigger core fund and a new growth fund. How do you think about adapting without losing what makes you Benchmark?

Peter Fenton: The craft that hasn’t changed is the core fund: working closely with founders at the beginning. It’s usually a 10-to-15-year commitment, [working] shoulder to shoulder, and that doesn’t scale. There’s also been inflation. We held the core fund at $500 million for 20 years, and it has just inflated to be consistent with the existing economy, which we hadn’t done and that was probably a tactical error on our part.

[As for the growth fund] it’s an expansion of our mandate. In some ways, we get permission from the ecosystem to do more than just the core early-stage business. [Not having this previously] was a fork in our eye. A number of opportunities that came to Benchmark would have returned somewhere between 10 and 1,000x to Benchmark, and we were constricted by our early-stage focus.
Are you thinking to make handful of bets with that $1.25 billion growth fund?

Fenton: We all have different answers, which is the beauty of a partnership. I’d love for us to have, as that great J.P. Morgan paper puts it, the agony and ecstasy of a concentrated portfolio. If the fund is successful, one or two investments will generate 90% of the returns. So I think it’s four to six, maybe seven to eight.
Ev, you’ve worked at Founders Fund, Bond, and Kleiner Perkins. How does Benchmark differ?

Ev Randall: Every firm is ultimately a collection of the people within the firm and how they work together. Some are very hierarchical, with a 50- or 60-person investment team and investment processes are federated into product groups. And then you have small partnerships. Very early in my career, I was drawn early to small partnerships because they allow a higher level of throughput and fidelity in your conversations, where you don’t feel like you’re making decisions through some Byzantine corporate structure. You’re going out on the field together, like a sports team going out on the field together.

And then the other piece is: You have to find your people, You have to find people who you not only like but admire. With Benchmark, with the current crop of GPs, it was obvious that everyone liked each other and got along, but it went deeper than that. It’s a group that admires each other and learns from each other. That mix of attributes is very rare, and when I saw it, I immediately wanted to join, and I think Jack felt the same way also as a newcomer.

Jack, you joined in February, but it was just a year ago that you raised a second, $275 million fund for your own firm in what you told the Wall Street Journal took one week. You have a hugely popular podcast. Why join Benchmark?

Jack Altman: It’s funny. I did the podcast with these guys at the start of this year, and during that podcast, obviously we talked about the commitment to being a small fund, but more than that, what I heard was that they want to be the first people who founders call, they want to be concentrated, and they just care. So much in this industry gets tied up in money and status, and what I felt from the Benchmark team then, and ten times more as I’ve gotten to know them so well, is it’s a group that really cares about founders and helping companies. And I did enjoy being an individual investor. . .but in a market this crazy, I don’t know how I’d feel, figuring it out on my own. Having a group of people who are so smart and focused and driven to learn it with and from has been awesome. There’s no better place to learn.
I’m told you meet on Mondays with no agenda.
Chethan Puttagunta: Jack tried to make an agenda. [Laughs.]
Altman: I’ve got an agenda for next Monday.

Eric Vishria: It’s weirdly arbitrary, honestly. It’s an ongoing conversation. In a time of rapid change, you’re trying to figure out what’s becoming possible that wasn’t possible six months ago, and who’s bending light. We talk about what companies we’re meeting, what piqued our interest and why, what we’re seeing in board meetings. You can try to systematize it, but one of the beauties of five people is you don’t have to. It’s a decades-long conversation that only works if you’re small and actually enjoy spending time together. After this session, we’re having dinner with one of the very few entrepreneurs who has built a multi-hundred-billion-dollar company, someone we’re not invested in, just to stretch our thinking.
Puttagunta: Part of not having an agenda is you need space to be reactive. If a founder needs help landing an executive or a strategic partnership, the five of us can be at their disposal.
You’re an equal partnership. Can one person put the kibosh on a deal?
Puttagunta: Nobody knows. We don’t have rules around it.
Altman: I actually don’t know. I was waiting to see what someone else did.
It’s never happened?

Altman: Because the firm is structured around a low volume of deals, you don’t actually want to have all of this rigor. If we invested in 100 or 200 companies a year, you’d want a CRM and a formal voting process. Because it’s so rare, the lack of structure is a huge asset.

Fenton: One of the differentiating aspects of our brand is we’re not so cocksure to come in and say ‘winner’ or ‘loser.’ It’s not Shark Tank. We sort of feel awe, for lack of a better term, at all the possibilities . . . The occasional case where someone comes in who’s polarizing — the entrepreneurs feel that. If someone in the room doesn’t like you, we’re not a great partner.
Companies are growing faster than ever. I’d think it’s easier to feel you’re missing out on opportunities if you don’t invest with greater frequency. Have you picked up the pace?

Puttagunta: I think the pace is consistent. I think part of the reality of venture capital in our business is that we are not going to be part of every successful company, and that’s okay. There are companies that we identify, we find that the entrepreneur has some great strength, and we want to amplify that strength. And it’s our job to find a way to work with that person. It kind of doesn’t matter how much capital they want to raise, or what structure, or where they are. You just have to work through all that stuff.

One thing that founders are interested in as a trend is VCs backing competing companies. Has that VC-founder pact changed because companies are growing so quickly and expanding into one another’s territory?

Vishria: One of the things we have an ethos around is, we are making a commitment to an entrepreneur, and through that commitment, we’re saying we’re going to work with you in this thing, and whatever that thing is, and we are working closely enough where it matters, and it should matter to them, and as it matters to us. The harsh reality of this world is every company is evolving very quickly, and so you do have companies that will naturally evolve from one thing to another, or pivot or change, and you are going to get conflicts. That’s just the reality of the of the kind of current dynamic. . .

Of course, we’re maintaining confidentiality and doing those things and fortunate to not end up in in that type of insane direct conflict [as happened recently with rival companies Factory and Cognition]. . . that commitment of exclusivity in that area is really important. But things are evolving. There’s no doubt about that.

Puttagunta: And I think people are ultra ambitious in this AI era. As the cost of coding new products effectively goes to zero, founders see a surface area and they want to attack the surface area, and so I think it’s probably going to happen more, where you start to run into each other. But there’s a way to be there’s a way to maintain that relationship and be respectful.
Jack, have you made an investment for Benchmark yet, and if so, did you feel a lot of pressure with that first deal?

Altman: I have, a few, and some are recent, so not all are disclosed. My background was software, but since joining, I’ve done chips, robotics and infra. Someone asked me when I joined, ‘How was the onboarding?’ And I was like, ‘It was perfect. There was no onboarding.’ Either Chethan or Eric told me early on, ‘Hey, you’re going to feel tight on your first one. Don’t. You’re going to make many investments while you’re here. This whole game includes crazy power laws. The odds of it being your first are low.’ . . . I trusted they understood what my shape was as a person, as an investor, and I was going to just try to stay as consistent to that as I could.

It really is a group dynamic on a lot of these. The investments I’ve made, I don’t think we would have won them if I didn’t have my partners. I don’t know that I would have been able to know how to get to a yes without them.
Eric, the AI chip company Cerebras was an unusual bet for Benchmark at the time it was made. What persuaded you to move forward with it?

Vishria: We invested in the spring of 2016, in the first round. We hadn’t made a hardware investment in 10 years. The founders seemed good, they had a very simple thesis, and I didn’t understand most of the rest. On the Sunday night before they came back to pitch the partnership, Peter told me it went against everything he’d learned in venture. Then, after the Monday pitch, he had flipped. A big part of it is understanding each other’s instincts. That began a journey of lots of ups and downs and many potential deaths of the company along the way, and it’s far from over. The romanticism of falling in love with a founder and an idea is why we do this.

Fenton: Andrew and his co-founders are heretics. What they were saying was unorthodox, and you see it today, with people dumping on the stock because it’s polarizing. That’s exactly where we have to be as investors. If it’s consensus, why is there a startup?
On that point, Cerebras priced at $185 when it went public earlier this year, jumped to $350, and is back near $185. Why?

Vishria: About six weeks before the IPO, I showed the company stock chart after stock chart: CoreWeave, Datadog, DoorDash, Amazon. Peak to trough, it’s insane how many of them move 500% in a year, up and down. So who knows? You control what you can control, and you update the public markets every 12 weeks. Being a public company takes a stomach of titanium, and the employees have to understand that.

Your former colleague, Bill Gurley, long argued that the traditional IPO process is broken, that that IPO pop benefits bankers and their clients — not the company. He’s a proponent of direct listings. Does anyone here agree with that thinking?

Vishria: I think maybe of this group, I’m the only one who’s worked on a direct listing. It can for sure make sense. I think the reality is for this crop of AI companies, it’s going to be unlikely because they need capital, and they need a lot of capital. At the end of the day, IPOs raise money. Cerebras raised $6 billion. That matters, so I think it’s probably unlikely for this crop just because most of them need capital.
Could a severe correction be coming? A lot of AI companies have exhausted free cash flow. It’s very expensive for companies to borrow. We also just saw the first AI bankruptcy with Character AI.

Randall: Macro is always a fool’s errand to predict with precision. What has changed most since I started investing is the information environment. Character.AI was the leftover corpse of a company whose founder and team were acqui-hired into Google a year and a half ago, and it was already sold for $2.3 billion; its Chapter 11 being read as an AI chill effect shows that the info environment for public equities in tech has been drawn so much into this, like, hyperactive X echo chamber.

If you look at the market today and you see where CoreWeave and Nebius and all these things are trading, those numbers are are due to the ARR figures of two private companies that will probably be public in the next 12 months . . .There’s so much capex and there’s so much investment that runs through the estimated and projected health of OpenAI and Anthropic.

Our companies see so much demand that they can’t get enough compute to serve customers who are willing to pay them at good gross margins. There’s nothing inherently unhealthy about the AI ecosystem. What’s unhealthy is the volatility from data points that are often untrue or exaggerated for clicks. I do think OpenAI and Anthropic going public would be healthy, so the market stops swinging 5% to 10% every time an anonymous account updates an estimate.
Those two companies have also really pulled the center of gravity back to San Francisco. Do you have to be in San Francisco to be a founder now? Are you interested in companies outside of California?

Altman: I don’t know that you have to be here as a founder, but I think it is right now by far the easiest place to get talent, capital, and customers. Probably everyone [on the team] works with companies that are not in San Francisco, but we’re also here in San Francisco every day, so I wouldn’t say you have to, but I’d say: strong bias for our particular setup.

Fenton: Historically, 90%-plus percent of the capital returns have come from companies founded here. There are beautiful stories outside that dense probability distribution — Shopify is a great example, Ramp — but the ecosystem effect that occurs when you have a successful company and that leads to a background of great executives [and] ambitious people, the bar of success gets raised. I don’t think it has systemically happened anywhere quite like here.

Randall: I’m trying to think of a non-SF based company that I’ve met with in the last 18 months that wasn’t actively saying that they were spending time in San Francisco. They’ve either opening an office in San Francisco, they’re spending half of their time in San Francisco, or they’re planning to move out to San Francisco. Iron sharpens iron. If you want to be around peers who are going to make you the best version of yourself, and it’s hard to think of a city that does that better than San Francisco in the current era that we’re in now with AI here.

articles.headline: Pierre Sage faces fight to save Crystal Palace job as dressing room concerns grow
keyFacts: Crystal Palace manager Pierre Sage faces a fight to save his job after a 5-0 defeat to Brighton.
TalkSPORT understands that dressing room concerns have grown and chairman Steve Parish previously held reservations about Sage.
Sage apologized to supporters and admitted the performance was his fault, leaving the team 14th in the Premier League.
body: Pierre Sage is facing a fight to save his job as Crystal Palace manager, talkSPORT understands.
It follows the Eagles’ 5-0 defeat to bitter rivals Brighton on Sunday afternoon.
Sage could be sacked less than four months after taking charge of Palace Getty
Palace have won just two of their opening seven Premier League matches under Sage this season.
The Frenchman was appointed on a three-year deal in the summer, replacing Oliver Glasner in the dugout.
However, Palace chairman Steve Parish held reservations over Sage heading into the recent international break.
Despite last weekend’s home win over Nottingham Forest, doubts still remain.
There are also concerns within the Palace dressing room following their heavy loss at Brighton.
The result leaves Sage’s side two points above the relegation zone in 14th place.
Sage apologised to supporters following the defeat at the Amex after his side were booed off the pitch by the travelling fans.
Speaking to BBC Sport at full-time, he admitted: “Only one feeling, shame. When you play this kind of game you have to show another face. It was our worst face.
“We cannot accept that, especially at the beginning of the game. We didn’t fight at this moment. Once it was 3-0 after nine minutes, the game is really different.
“Especially in the way we don’t understand in which context we were. In this kind of game you need different ingredients.
Sage’s side were booed off following a 5-0 thrashing by Brighton Getty
“It’s my fault because I am the coach, I gave the angle to the players. I gave the motivation. I prepare the situations. We played so badly. It’s my fault.
“I don’t want to speak really individually or thinking about details. I have to analyse what’s happened to take a decision.
“At this moment, once the score is [large difference], it’s easier to play. It’s about bravery. We have to deal with these things from the beginning of the game.”
Palace suffered a catastrophic start to the afternoon as they conceded three goals inside the opening 10 minutes.
Those included an own goal from Jaydee Canvot just four minutes into the match.
Diego Gomez then added a second for the hosts from the halfway line.
Sage apologised to Palace fans following their latest defeat Getty
Yasin Ayari, Charalampos Kostoulas and Jack Hinshelwood were also on the scoresheet.
The result marks only the second time Brighton have scored five against Palace and the first instance since 1956.

articles.headline: Madueke's 'anger and conviction' shows he's more than a 'finisher'
keyFacts: Substitute Noni Madueke scored the winning goal in the second half to give Arsenal a 1-0 victory over Nottingham Forest.
Manager Mikel Arteta praised Madueke for showing increased anger and conviction in his recent performances following a hamstring injury to teammate Christos Tzolis.
Arsenal substitutes have contributed to 26 Premier League goals since the start of last season, which is more than any other team in the league.
body: - Published
Noni Madueke may not have the starting role he wants at Arsenal, but his winning goal against Nottingham Forest showed why he is one of Mikel Arteta's valued "finishers".
The England international scored in the second half to earn Arsenal a 1-0 result and three valuable points towards their defence of the Premier League title.
Madueke has started just one top-flight game this season, the 2-1 win over Leeds that came eight days prior to their victory over Oliver Glasner's Forest on Sunday.
Arsenal's summer was dominated by talk of their search for an elite forward, with the left wing one of the positions identified.

But after unsuccessful pursuits of superstar players such as Vinicius Jr and Julian Alvarez, the only new addition in that position was Christos Tzolis, the winger brought in to replace the outgoing Leandro Trossard.

Tzolis has started the season well and has been the first-choice winger for Arteta, meaning that Madueke and Eberechi Eze have had to be content with the majority of their minutes coming from the bench or in the Carabao Cup.

However, Tzolis is now out with a hamstring injury picked up while playing for Greece, and that has presented a chance for Madueke to show Arteta why he should be considering the former Chelsea man as much more than a finisher - the term Arteta uses for his substitutes.

Madueke did well when starting against Leeds, praised by Arteta for being the best player at the club during the international break. The Arsenal boss said the winger "grabbed it [his start] with both hands".
The England international also started on the right wing, his more natural position, against Lille in a Champions League win on Tuesday, assisting the opening goal.
Against Forest on Sunday, Madueke was introduced at half-time by Arteta and said he took the manager's instructions with him on to the pitch.
"Hang in there, stick to the gameplan, go out there and try to attack the opposition, be dangerous, be yourself and be good defensively as well," Madueke said.
He scored with a deflected shot in the 80th minute when he took on defender Daniel Munoz and cut in on his weaker right foot.
"I'd beaten him on the outside a couple of times so I thought I'll come inside and just let rip," Madueke said.
'He is a special character'
It's fair to say that the Arsenal fans have not always taken to Madueke since his move from London rivals Chelsea.
There was a 'No to Madueke' petition started when he joined the club and his performances have been criticised for being inconsistent.
But since his Â£48.5m arrival, Madueke has helped the club lift their first Premier League title in 22 years and played a big part as Arsenal reached the Champions League final.
Madueke scored eight goals and provided four assists in 43 appearances in all competitions last season, but questions over his end product remain.
He is one of Arsenal's most direct players, and England manager Thomas Tuchel and his staff also rate the winger as one of the best players in one-versus-one situations.
"Noni, look at me, a smile on my face because he is a special character," Arteta said when he was asked about Madueke's character.
"It's someone that's very much loved in and around the dressing room. The way he connects, talks with people. He is just a special guy.
"I think I saw an interview where they were asking a few of our players 'who would you call if you had a problem?' And some of them said Noni, which I was surprised.
"But I think it is a massive credit and describes the type of person he is."
The 24-year-old has now put in three good performances in a row.

"He is in a good moment," Arteta said. "After the break, he is showing something else, another level of anger, another level of conviction as well as in his actions and he is becoming decisive in matches, which is what we expect from a player like him.
"He is a player that doesn't really mind left or right, but he has played many more minutes on the right side. The team needs him there at the moment and he is doing well."
Arsenal's 'finishers' continue to get the job done
Arteta has made a big point of referring to his substitutes as "finishers" as he points to the importance of the squad.
That mentality is seeming to have the desired effect. Since the start of last season, Arsenal substitutes have contributed to 26 Premier League goals, which is more than any other side in the league.

Bruno Guimaraes scored the winner against Leeds after coming off the bench last time out in the league, while substitutes Bukayo Saka, Kai Havertz and captain Martin Odegaard played a major role in the last two goals in the win over Lille.
But Arteta is not concerned the Gunners are overly reliant on players from the bench.
"There have been other games as well that we have had to score in the first half," Arteta said.
"We have played 11 competitive matches and we won 10. We are getting a variety of ways to win in many different contexts."

Arteta said he expected few chances against a well organised Forest at the City Ground but added: "I had the belief that the moment the physical level was going to drop, the spaces would be a little bit bigger, the timing more and we would be more efficient there.
"And the finishers delivered because the context of the game changed a little bit."

articles.headline: Battlefield 6 devs to fix "Secuty" skin typo, but five-pistol outfit was intentional
keyFacts: Battlefield Studios announced that a typo reading 'Secuty' on a Battlefield 6 Season 5 skin will be fixed in an upcoming correction update.
The studio stated that a separate skin featuring five pistols was an intentional creative concept inspired by action movie tropes.
Battlefield Studios did not address fan accusations that generative AI was used to create the cosmetics.
body: Battlefield Studios has responded after fans accused it of using AI to generate cosmetics after spotting a "Secuty" typo on a Battlefield 6 Season 5 skin.
The studio acknowledged "candid feedback" from players in a statement on social media, insisting it had "hear[d] your concerns".

And though the statement did not mention AI - either to admit or deny using the generative tech - BattlefieldComm said that while the 'Secuty' typo will be addressed by a "correction update", an outfit with five pistols is intentional.

"First, let's dive into the 'Secuty' typo patches on the McNeil character," the studio wrote. "A correction update has already been planned for the Season 5 Phase 2 release. However, we recognise that letting a known visual error go live without quick acknowledgement creates confusion and erodes trust. We are reviewing how we communicate known visual bugs so you aren’t left wondering whether something was intentional or overlooked."

The five-pistol-touting Midnight Mirage skin, however, is described as an "intentional creative concept" and "a nod to over-the-top action movie tropes where an operative inexplicably has another backup weapon strapped to every spare inch of gear".

"That said, we understand how this could look unintentional when released alongside other cosmetic anomalies," the team added, and, specifically addressing the typo, said: "We take pride in the craft of our world and our gear, and seeing visual oddities slip through is frustrating for everyone."
Cosmetic Quality & Recent Feedback
Over the past week, we’ve seen conversation, memes, and candid feedback around a few of our latest skins and cosmetic items—specifically the standard issue McNeil skin with “SECUTY” typo.
You called it out clearly, and we hear your concerns.…
— Battlefield Comms (@BattlefieldComm) October 16, 2026
The message did not say how the typo happened or address fan accusations that generative AI was used.

Season 5 launched in Battlefield 6 this week as planned, and though most of the new additions - new maps, weapons and vehicles, and gameplay changes - were well received, the season began on a low note due to those aforementioned accusations of generative AI use and a major hit to XP gain.

articles.headline: Anthropic gives outside AI watchdog “employee-like” access
keyFacts: Anthropic granted nonprofit evaluator METR employee-like access to its systems to assess risks of its artificial intelligence models.
The announcement marks the first step in implementing a proposal backed by rivals Sam Altman and Elon Musk.
Critics argued third-party evaluators create conflicts of interest, while Anthropic said public sharing could benefit malicious actors.
body: Anthropic has granted external evaluators “employee-like access” to assess the risks of its models, following through on a commitment to increase safeguards over concerns the technology could run catastrophically out of control.

METR, a nonprofit that has worked with leading labs including OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and Meta, now has a team embedded in the Claude maker’s office with access to its hardware and internal systems.

A greater role for third-party evaluators is among the main concrete steps the labs have proposed in response to rising concern about the dangers more capable AI systems could pose to the economy, cyber security and humanity at large.

Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei achieved a rare moment of unity with arch-rivals Sam Altman and Elon Musk in September when the OpenAI and SpaceX bosses rallied behind his proposal to embed external auditors in the leading labs.
Thursday’s announcement marks the first step to implementing these pledges. OpenAI has yet to lay out plans to bring in evaluators after Altman said Amodei’s proposals were a good idea.

“As models have become more powerful, they’ve required stronger safeguards and more challenging risk assessment,” Anthropic said on Thursday. “We want to be publicly accountable for the decisions we’re making. But we can’t publicly share all the information relevant to our safety work.”

Critics of Anthropic’s proposal to use evaluators have argued the arrangements could lead to conflicts of interest, pointing to issues in the accounting sector, and that greater government regulation is required.

Anthropic argued that sharing information publicly could benefit malicious actors or competitors and added that its evaluators will operate similarly to bank supervision, whereby regulators assign resident examiners to work inside the largest banks.

articles.headline: Scientists Find a ‘Ghostly Green’ Star, and That’s Not the Only Crazy Color
keyFacts: Scientists discovered that white dwarf stars can produce unexpected colors like green, pink, cyan, yellow, and purple, according to a recent study.
Lead author Mark Hollands and his team simulated human vision for 151 white dwarfs, identifying what is likely the first green star ever discovered.
Hollands said most of these stars will shift back to normal colors after a few million years as gravity pulls trace elements inward.
body: High school science class taught us that stars come in very specific colors. You have cooler stars that are red, orange and yellow. Then you have hotter, larger stars that are white and blue. It turns out that much like the wind in the movie Pocahontas, stars also come in all sorts of colors, including green and pink.

The discovery was outlined in a study published this month in RAS Techniques and Instruments. According to the lead author, Mark Hollands of Warwick University’s astronomy and astrophysics group, the humble white dwarf star is the centerpiece of this chromatic curiosity.

“Most stars, including most white dwarfs, behave like ‘perfect radiators,’ so their color is set almost entirely by temperature. But nobody had really looked into what else might be possible for white dwarfs,” Hollands said in a statement. “It turns out these incredibly dense stars can produce colors nobody expected, and some of them genuinely surprised me.”
More from CNET

Hollands says that the key is density and atmosphere. White dwarfs are among the densest objects in the known universe, and that also includes the atmosphere around the white dwarf. Thanks to the intense gravity, a white dwarf’s atmosphere — which is composed primarily of hydrogen and helium — can have some interesting interactions with trace amounts of other elements that are present.

“For white dwarfs with a cool, helium-dominated atmosphere, as the star gets cooler, the helium becomes more and more transparent, which means you can see further into the star where the gas gets denser,” Hollands told CNET in an email. “When you have trace elements in the star, whether it’s metals like sodium and calcium from a planetary system, or carbon from the core, they interact with the dense helium.”

These interactions cause the trace elements to absorb light across the wavelength, for a wider range of “missing” colors. The result is a white dwarf that could appear in any number of colors based on what trace elements it absorbed.
So, there are green stars out there?

That is precisely what Hollands and his team found in their research. To date, no one has ever seen a white dwarf star with human eyes, and none is close enough to be seen directly. Most analysis of a star is done with spectroscopy, so scientists know what a star is made of and how bright it is. Typically, scientists focus more on the science and things like chemical makeup and brightness, rather than color.

“As astronomers, we spend more time thinking about the technical questions about physics,” Hollands said. “It’s a very simple question to ask, ‘what do these stars actually look like when you visit them,’ something I see members of the public ask all the time. It turns out it wasn’t actually too difficult to answer.”

Hollands and his team used the same data for 151 white dwarf stars and ran it through a simulation that converted it to human color vision. Of those, 146 were pretty normal, averaging about 6,800K in color temperature. These would appear bright white to humans, with maybe the tiniest hint of blue.

The other five results were a lot more interesting: The team found examples of cyan, yellow, purple/violet, pink and, yes, even green. The green star is called WD J1330+6435, and it is a white dwarf that sits in a rocky planetary system. The debris from that system gets pulled into the star, lending it the trace elements needed to turn a “ghostly green,” per Hollands.

Another interesting find was WDJ0902+2010, a star that has a ton of carbon in its atmosphere. According to the study, this cooler white dwarf churns up carbon from its innards, and the carbon in the atmosphere absorbs light across the spectrum. It results in a star that would appear salmon-pink to humans.

Since the researchers could find no other credible reports of a green star being discovered before, WD J1330+6435 is likely the first green star ever discovered. Hollands said that the pink and cyan colors were also likely firsts, as there aren’t any reports of astronomers finding stars in those colors either.

Unfortunately, the stars won’t stay in these colors forever. Hollands says that white dwarfs start out intensely hot — about 100,000 degrees Kelvin — which would give them a “sky blue color.” This changes as the white dwarf cools, and you only get the really cool colors when it reaches about 5,000K or so. Eventually, the high gravity will pull the trace elements into the core of the star, changing it back to its normal white or orange colors.

The lone exception is the pink star. Since its carbon already comes from within the star, the star’s natural convection forces are causing that color. That means WDJ0902+2010 is likely to remain pink for billions of years, whereas the rest will likely shift back to their natural colors after a few million years.

articles.headline: Fire Emblem’s Remarkable Comeback
keyFacts: Nintendo's Fire Emblem franchise once faced potential cancellation due to declining sales and franchise fatigue.
The development team stated that Fire Emblem Awakening needed to sell 250,000 copies or the series would end.
Fire Emblem Awakening became a massive hit by adding a Casual mode, saving the series and leading to continued future success.
body: Though it may not be a sales juggernaut on the scale of Mario or The Legend of Zelda, Fire Emblem is one of Nintendo's preeminent franchises. Like so many of its vaunted stablemates, the series is almost as old as Nintendo's gaming ambitions, debuting on the Famicom and appearing on nearly every home and handheld console since. Given this prominence, it's almost difficult to believe that Fire Emblem's future was ever in jeopardy, but such was indeed once the case; there was a point in time when the series was very much on the verge of cancellation, and it took a dramatic shakeup to reverse its fortunes.

To fully contextualize this rocky period in Fire Emblem's history, we need to look back at its trajectory in the wake of its belated international debut. Unlike Nintendo's other marquee properties, Fire Emblem took a circuitous route to Western markets. Though the series began in 1990, its first several installments were never released outside of Japan, and most Western players would end up being introduced to the franchise not through one of its mainline entries, but through Super Smash Bros. Melee for the Nintendo GameCube.

Even more so than its predecessor, Melee was a veritable celebration of Nintendo history. The game drew deeply from the company's rich oeuvre; its roster was stuffed with beloved mascots, and its extensive array of collectible trophies covered the full sweep of the publisher's gaming legacy, from renowned classics to obscure curios. What generated the most chatter among international players, however, were two particular hidden fighters who hailed from a series most had never heard of: Marth, hero of the first Fire Emblem , and Roy, protagonist of the series' then-newest installment, The Binding Blade.

Despite their unfamiliarity, these mysterious swordsmen instantly became two of Melee's most popular characters thanks to their cool designs and nimble swordplay, which helped set them apart from the more recognizable characters on the roster. More consequentially, their newfound popularity among Western players generated immediate interest in Fire Emblem as a whole–a series that, to that point, had been all but unknown outside of Japan. That the franchise was notable enough to warrant not one, but two representatives in Melee was yet more indication of its significance, and only further stoked players' curiosity.
Marth in Super Smash Bros. Ultimate

This upswell in interest (coupled with the critical and commercial success of Fire Emblem's sister series Advance Wars, which likewise had just made its worldwide debut after a similarly long period of Japan exclusivity) went a long way in encouraging Nintendo to finally bring the franchise to other markets, beginning with its next GBA installment (and seventh entry overall), Fire Emblem: The Blazing Blade . The gambit paid off; thanks to its wider availability, Blazing Blade became the first game in the series to sell more than 800,000 copies, solidifying it as another tentpole franchise for the company and ensuring there would be no hesitation to bring future titles westward.

The next few Fire Emblem games saw similar commercial success. The series' second worldwide release (and final GBA installment), The Sacred Stones , arrived in 2005 and moved more than 700,000 copies over its lifetime, while GameCube's Path of Radiance followed later that same year and sold more than half a million copies–well enough to satisfy Nintendo's expectations, considering the system's age and comparatively small user base.

Gradually, however, the series experienced diminishing returns. Fire Emblem: Radiant Dawn , a direct sequel to Path of Radiance, arrived on the Wii in 2007 and ultimately sold fewer copies than its predecessor, despite the fervor surrounding the console at the time. Fire Emblem: Shadow Dragon , a DS remake of the original 1990 game, followed in 2008 to a similarly muted reception. While the dual-screen handheld had a significantly larger install base than the Game Boy Advance, Shadow Dragon moved an estimated 600,000 copies–a significant drop off from both GBA titles. In the face of this downward trend, Nintendo elected not to localize the series' next DS entry, New Mystery of the Emblem–the first time in nearly a decade that a Fire Emblem game would not be released outside of Japan.

As with some of Nintendo's other aging franchises from around the same period, franchise fatigue was beginning to set in for Fire Emblem. The relatively quick succession of releases, none of which deviated very far from the series' well-worn formula, coupled with their steep difficulty and lack of innovation, led to a steadily dwindling audience. So persistent was the decline that the long-running franchise now found itself at risk of cancellation; according to the development team, the next Fire Emblem would be the last if it failed to sell at least 250,000 copies, which prompted some radical proposals for how to shake the series up.
Fire Emblem Awakening

The resulting game, Fire Emblem Awakening , did not completely upend fan expectations, but it did become a massive hit, saving the entire series . Rather than reinventing the franchise, Awakening was developed as a "grand culmination" of it, tweaking the established formula in inspired ways and reworking staid conventions. The game leaned heavily on the series' character-driven nature, placing an even greater emphasis on character development and relationships than previous titles. But perhaps even more consequential was the addition of a Casual mode–a feature that originated in New Mystery of the Emblem but had never previously appeared in an international release. Casual mode effectively turned off one of Fire Emblem's hallmark mechanics, permadeath–a move that once felt tantamount to sacrilege, but had a profound impact on the series' approachability. With the option to disable permadeath, the game became much more welcoming; now that there were no long-term repercussions for a miscalculated move, players could enjoy the complex narrative and deep gameplay without worrying about irreversible consequences, opening the series up to a much wider audience than before.

Awakening would go on to sell more than two million copies, kickstarting a resurgence for the series. Each subsequent entry would build upon Awakening's experimental streak, evolving the franchise in unexpected ways. Fire Emblem Fates followed in 2015 and was an even bigger hit, moving more than three million copies. In a page out of Pokemon's playbook, Fates released in three separate versions, presenting the same tale from three alternate perspectives. Two years later, the series made its mobile debut with Fire Emblem Heroes , which would go on to become Nintendo's most successful mobile game, while its final 3DS installment, Fire Emblem Echoes: Shadows of Valentia , followed a few months later and surpassed a million copies over its lifetime.

Fire Emblem has continued to prosper in the years since, with Switch's Three Houses setting a new benchmark for the series with over four million copies sold. Thanks to an eventual willingness to innovate and rethink long-standing conventions, the storied RPG was able to weather declining sales and the looming threat of cancellation to become one of Nintendo's stalwart franchises, offering an incisive lesson in how to steward a long-running series. And with the positive reception that's greeted the newly released Fortune's Weave , it appears Fire Emblem will continue to occupy a vital place in Nintendo's pantheon for a long time to come.

articles.headline: The dark side of optimizing fertility
keyFacts: Some prospective parents use polygenic screening to test embryos for complex diseases and physical traits, author Kristen V. Brown said.
Most mainstream medical societies and IVF doctors oppose polygenic embryo screening because they believe it lacks value, Brown said.
Embryo editing is currently illegal in the United States and most countries, though interest in the technology is growing, Brown said.
body: A gynecologist points to the head of a fetus in an ultrasound image. | Jan Woitas/picture alliance via Getty Images

We live in an era of endless optimization. Fitness trackers help us measure our lifespan, people are consuming piles of protein in an attempt to be their best selves, and there’s even an urge to maximize our morality . In a world of constant self-improvement, it’s no wonder that journey has reached our attempts at reproduction.

Kristen V. Brown is a journalist and author of the forthcoming book The Immortal Womb: The Centuries-Long Quest to Control the Female Body and Hack Human Reproduction . As the title suggests, she writes about all of the ways people are trying to exert more control over the process of having children.

“I think that what we’re seeing right now is that people will do anything they can to have the healthiest baby possible,” she told Vox. “So much is out of your control, and people are just trying to figure out, how do I get more control? How do I skew the odds in my favor?” She says that one way people try to get more agency is through a technology called PGT-P, or preimplantation genetic testing for polygenic risk.

“If you go through IVF, very often they’ll have you do a basic genetic screening that can detect things like Down syndrome. This screening takes that up a notch,” Brown said. “It uses that same preimplantation genetic testing to look for the likelihood of complex genetic conditions — stuff like heart disease, like diabetes — in order to, quote, ‘let people have the healthiest baby.’”

But what can potential parents do with that knowledge? How far can this technology go? And what are the ethics of using it in the first place? We discuss that and more on the latest episode of Explain It to Me , Vox’s weekly call-in podcast.

Below is an excerpt of my conversation with Brown, edited for length and clarity. You can listen to the full episode on Apple Podcasts , Spotify , or wherever you get your podcasts. If you’d like to submit a question, send an email to askvox@vox.com or call 1-800-618-8545.
What other things are they testing embryos for?

For conditions that are only impacted by one gene, like Huntington’s disease, it’s very easy to say, ‘Does this embryo have it or not?’ with a pretty good degree of confidence. But that’s not how this technology works. Something like heart disease, for example, is impacted by hundreds of genes. Also, something like heart disease is not only genetic. It’s affected by environment and lifestyle.

I think that what’s motivating most people is the health aspect. But a lot of these companies are marketing these tests, saying they can also look for height. They can look at eye color. Some of them are promising IQ. How do you even define intelligence, let alone how do you define the genetics of intelligence? Alzheimer’s disease, longevity, which embryo is going to live the longest life. So it’s already gone beyond disease into some of these more aesthetic concerns.
Do we know how many people are doing this?
I think it’s a very small number of people at this point. But I think that we’re seeing more and more companies in the space, and we’re seeing more and more support from fertility doctors.

I want to emphasize that most mainstream medical societies are against this. Most of the IVF doctors I know do not think this has value. Most people in the genetic space do not think this technology has value either for embryos or for adults, but I think we’re seeing support growing.
I think that a lot of people in the fertility space are already envisioning a future where this does become more mainstream because the idea is just so appealing, even if the technology has flaws.
What about embryo editing? Is that something we’re seeing? Can people go in and change things around?

Not right now. Embryo editing is very much illegal in the United States. It is illegal in most countries. How can you be sure enough that it’s safe? Because you won’t know for sure until an embryo grows up into an adult whether anything went awry.

Right now it is illegal, but there is growing interest as the technology has gotten better. Most of the support right now for embryo editing is for disease. The argument for it is that, let’s say you are a carrier for Huntington’s disease or you have Huntington’s disease. Right now, there is something that you can do. You can use polygenic screening to select the embryos that don’t have the disease, but in IVF, even if you don’t have a terrible disease hiding in your DNA, it’s hard to get a lot of embryos.

You have these situations where couples have to do rounds and rounds and rounds of IVF to get one or two embryos that aren’t carriers for a harmful variant, right? And so the argument for it is, let’s give these people a better shot.
But I imagine there are people out there who aren’t looking into editing simply for making children more resistant to diseases. They are looking at those things like eye color and height.

There’s actually a name for that. This tech executive called Brian Armstrong coined this term, the Gattaca stack, [named] after the movie. The vision is to use a suite of fertility technologies to make the perfect human.

The first thing they want to use is this technology called in vitro gametogenesis, which is where you take a skin cell and you turn it into an egg and a sperm, and then you make an embryo with it, so women don’t have to go through rounds of IVF.
The idea is that you can get tons and tons and tons of embryos, and then you can use PGT-P to then screen for the best ones, and then you can use an artificial womb to incubate and grow them.
This brings to mind a certain E word, and that word is eugenics. What are the ethics here?

Because on one hand, I can understand that there are parents who are like, “I just want to have a healthy baby. I want to bring a child into this world. I just want to put my best foot forward with this human that I’m going to bring to Earth.” And then on the other hand, it gets a little weird.

It gets weird fast. In some ways, we’ve already gone down that slippery slope. Right now, even if you don’t go through IVF, we screen against Down syndrome early in pregnancy. Down syndrome is a condition in which you have a disability, but you can live a full, happy, healthy life. For a long time, parents of kids with Down syndrome have argued that already selecting and screening against Down syndrome pregnancies is a form of [eugenics].

As technology gets more advanced, we see that same question applied to more and more conditions. I think that one of the things that we don’t talk about enough is that the genome is complicated. You can’t actually just go in there and be like, ‘I want a tall baby with blue eyes and a great laugh.’

I think that becoming a parent is an exercise in giving up control, and that’s easier for some people than others. I have so much sympathy and empathy for people who are trying to stack the deck. But I think there are just so many variables when it comes to human reproduction that we are never going to be able to fully control the process, as much as we might want to and as appealing as that might sound.

articles.headline: U.S. taking Putin’s side would be a ‘historic mistake,’ says Zelenskyy
keyFacts: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned that U.S. President Donald Trump formally siding with Russia would be a historic mistake.
Trump defended his decision to waive new sanctions against Russia, stating it was in U.S. national interests to address fuel costs and keep Russia at the bargaining table.
Zelenskyy reported that recent disruptions in U.S. intelligence sharing had been resolved, though restrictions on Starlink technology remained in place.
body: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has warned that the U.S.’ formally siding with Russia’s Vladimir Putin would be a “historic mistake” but said he still sees President Donald Trump as an ally despite a series of moves that have unsettled his country and its friends on Capitol Hill.

“We want to trust him,” Zelenskyy told NBC News’ “Meet the Press” on Sunday, referring to Trump. “I hope that he will change his decisions, because I think that it’s all mistakes, and it will not help us, and it will not help United States.”

Trump on Friday waived sweeping new sanctions against Russia passed by Congress, saying in an executive order that the move “is in the national interests of the United States.” Passed with bipartisan support and signed by Trump last month, the sanctions were intended to target Russia’s revenue streams by punishing global buyers of Russian oil and gas.

Trump defended his decision Sunday, writing on Truth Social that he did not want to “drive, foolishly, Russia away from the bargaining table.” Trump added that Zelenskyy was targeting diesel refineries in Russia, which he claimed was “seriously hurting the world diesel markets, including those in the United States.”

Trump added that “Russia is doing very little, if anything, to help the Islamic Republic of Iran, compared to what they could be doing, and I want to keep it that way, and will, unless stupid people get in the way,” a claim that comes the same day the Russian Foreign Affairs Ministry announced that Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov would travel to Tehran this week.
The waiver came days after a deal with Putin to release hundreds of thousands of tons of Russian diesel fuel onto the global market as fuel prices soar was announced.

At the same time, Zelenskyy said, U.S. intelligence sharing was briefly “blocked,” blinding Ukraine to incoming ballistic missiles, while limits have been placed on Starlink technology critical to intercept jet-powered drones.
Zelenskyy told moderator Kristen Welker that Ukrainian officials believe the decision to limit Starlink, imposed by Elon Musk’s SpaceX, came in response to a “message from American government.”

The U.S. has been Ukraine’s most significant backer across 4½ years of war, but personal relations between Trump and Zelenskyy have appeared severely strained in recent weeks, with each publicly criticizing the other.
Asked about Trump’s remark last week that he was “more difficult to deal with than Putin,” Zelenskyy said he was “very honest” with Trump.
“Maybe it’s not very polite,” he said, but it is “better to have partners who are very open and clear than to have those who are killers, even with a smile on their face.”
Zelenskyy, who accused the U.S. of betraying Kyiv last week, said his feelings have not changed. He warned that Trump’s diesel deal with Russia “will strengthen Putin in his will to occupy us.”
Announcing the deal last week, Trump expressed hopes that it would go some way to address soaring fuel costs.
But Zelenskyy said the deal wouldn’t have “a real influence” on the price of oil in the U.S. because the rising prices were due to the blockage of the Strait of Hormuz, not Ukraine.
“I don’t know all the reasons why President Trump makes such deals,” he said.
Of the prospect of the U.S.’ more formally siding with Russia, he said: “If these two countries will be together ... we will not prevail, and we will not be able to stand.”
Zelenskyy said it was a “pity” Trump had waived the sanctions in a bill named for the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, R-S.C., who he said was “a great supporter of peace and of Ukraine.”
“He invested his life and time because he really believed in Ukraine,” he said.
In a separate interview on “Meet the Press,” Sen. James Lankford, R-Okla., defended Trump’s decision to lift the Russia sanctions.

“He’s trying to walk this fine balance between trying to be able to put pressure on Russia, but also to be able to help the American people, so he is choosing the American people first is what he’s doing,” Lankford said, pointing to high gas prices.

Asked whether Trump’s moves indicate the president is siding with Putin, Lankford, a member of the Intelligence Committee, said Trump was “siding with the free people of Ukraine,” adding later that Trump was working to get the two countries “to the table to be able to negotiate.”

The war has seen little recent movement on the front line, with Russia continuing to occupy around a fifth of Ukraine. Trump had vowed to end the conflict within days of the start of his second term, but peace talks have effectively stalled, with Ukraine saying that Russia has rejected a short-term ceasefire and that Putin’s terms for peace are tantamount to a full surrender.
Meanwhile, another difficult winter looms for Ukrainian civilians, with a critical munitions shortage limiting Zelenskyy’s ability to defend infrastructure against Russian strikes.

Zelenskyy said he was due to speak to U.S. negotiators by phone later Sunday and was still hopeful of a meeting in the days ahead. “I’m very open for this, even with all the difficult circumstances,” he said.
He cited some progress after a multiday interruption in U.S. intelligence about incoming Russian ballistic missiles, which he said has now been “deblocked.”
“We are very thankful for this,” he said. “Now it works.”

European and Ukrainian officials previously told NBC News they believed that a move to limit sharing intelligence, coming only days after Trump eased sanctions on Russia, was most likely aimed at pressuring Kyiv to make concessions at the negotiating table amid a stalemate in peace talks.

While Zelenskyy indicated that the intelligence problem has been resolved, he said Ukraine was still facing an ongoing speed restriction on its use of Starshield, the military version of the Starlink service.

Asked whether he thought Trump or Musk had directly made the decision to limit Starlink, Zelenskyy said he did not know but thought “both” were involved. He said that if Trump decided tomorrow to lift the restriction, “it will immediately work as it was before.”
The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
